sections.h2: What makes Dane County property tax different from other Wisconsin counties?
sections.html:
Dane County is large, urban and split between many taxing bodies, and one city, Madison, collects its own current-year tax. The 2020 census counted 561,504 residents, which made Dane the second most populous county in Wisconsin after Milwaukee County, with nearly 10% of the state's people.

Madison is both the county seat and the state capital. The county covers 1,238 square miles, of which 1,197 are land. It was formed in 1836, organized in 1839, and named for Nathan Dane, a Massachusetts delegate who helped carve Wisconsin out of the Northwest Territory. Interstates 39, 90 and 94 cross it, along with U.S. 12, 14, 18, 51 and 151.

Housing is split between owners and renters. In 2020 there were 248,795 housing units and 238,417 households, and 56.3% of occupied units were owner-occupied against 43.7% rented. About 86.4% of residents lived in urban areas. The homeowner vacancy rate was 0.8% and the rental vacancy rate 3.9%.

The county's municipalities include:

  • Cities: Fitchburg, Madison, Middleton, Monona, Stoughton, Sun Prairie, Verona and Edgerton (mostly in Rock County).
  • Villages: Belleville, Black Earth, Blue Mounds, Brooklyn, Cambridge, Cottage Grove, Cross Plains, Dane, Deerfield, DeForest, Maple Bluff, Marshall, Mazomanie, McFarland, Mount Horeb, Oregon, Rockdale, Shorewood Hills, Waunakee and Windsor.
  • Many towns, from Albion and Berry to Westport and York, each with its own board and assessor.

sections.h2: When are Dane County property taxes due?
sections.html:
The first due date is January 31 and the final due date is July 31. Local municipalities mail bills on the third Monday of December, and Access Dane is updated with the new tax information the same day.

The county treasurer explains the cycle this way. Assessors set values as of January 1. Taxing districts set budgets in the fall. In December the tax is calculated from each assessment and the levies of the overlying districts. The calculation is assessment times mill rate for total taxes, minus the lottery credit and first dollar credit for net property taxes, plus special assessments and special charges for the bill itself.

DateEventPay to
January 1Municipal assessor determines valuesNone
Spring or summerNotice of Assessment, Open Book, then Board of ReviewLocal clerk and assessor
Third Monday of DecemberBills mailed by the local municipalityNone
January 31First due dateLocal municipality
July 31Final due dateDane County Treasurer, except City of Madison properties

Source: Dane County Treasurer, Property Tax 101.

The treasurer reports roughly how owners pay: about 30% pay in full in December, about 40% pay in full in January, and about 30% pay in installments. Madison differs because its bills have intermediate installments and the City Treasurer collects through the July 31 date. The Madison treasurer is at 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Room 107, phone (608) 266-4771.

sections.h2: What happens if a Dane County tax payment is late?
sections.html:
The whole bill comes due at once, and combined interest and penalty of 1.5% of the unpaid principal is added back to February 1. The charge accrues at the start of each month until principal, interest and penalty are paid in full.

The treasurer gives a worked example. An owner who is late with the final installment still owes the charge going back to February 1, so a payment in August carries seven months of it, or 10.5%. After that, each month adds another 1.5% to the outstanding principal.

Timeliness depends on the postmark, and the county warns that the Postal Service does not postmark mail the day it is dropped off. Practical options near a deadline:

  • Pay in person at the City-County Building, Room 114, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison. The office is open 8:00 to 4:00 Monday through Friday, excluding holidays, and has a drop box.
  • Pay by e-Check or credit card on the Treasurer's website.
  • Mail a check to Dane County Treasurer, PO Box 1299, Madison, WI 53701-1299, early enough to be postmarked on time.
  • If you pay through your bank, schedule it 7 to 10 business days ahead.

Delinquent taxes need a separate check to Dane County. A payment is not valid until it clears the bank, and a returned payment cancels the bills it covered.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Dane County assessment?
sections.html:
Talk to your municipal assessor first, then go to the municipal Board of Review if you still disagree. The county treasurer notes that after the Board of Review it is normally too late to appeal the assessed value for that year.

The Notice of Assessment usually arrives in March or later. The Open Book period lets an owner discuss the numbers with the assessor, and the Board of Review hears formal appeals in a quasi-judicial setting. Wisconsin Statute 70.47 sets several firm rules:

  • The board meets within the 45-day period beginning the fourth Monday of April.
  • An owner must give notice at least 48 hours ahead and then file a written objection in the first two hours of the first meeting, unless the board waives the rule.
  • An owner who refused a reasonable certified-mail request from the assessor to view the exterior cannot appear before the board.
  • For property valued by the income method, the owner must send the assessor requested income and expense data no later than 7 days before the first meeting.
  • If the board waives the hearing, the owner has 60 days from the notice of waiver to start an excessive assessment action under Statute 74.37(3)(d).

The treasurer's page also links the Wisconsin Department of Revenue Guide for Property Owners and the Board of Review Member Guide. Each city, village and town runs its own board, so the local clerk tells you the date.

sections.h2: What if a Dane County property has already gone to tax deed?
sections.html:
A former owner can repurchase before the public auction, and the county sells what it acquired as is. Dane County does not sell tax deeds or tax liens. It sells properties it acquired through the tax deed process under Wisconsin Statute 75.35.

Auctions are usually held in October or November, and sometimes again in April or May. They use sealed bids. The bid due date is a Tuesday at 1:00 pm, and the bid opening is the next day at 10:00 am in the Treasurer's office. Each bid needs a form and a 10% earnest deposit. Payment is by cash or cashier's check only, and the buyer has ten days after the award notice to complete the purchase.

For former owners, repurchase is possible up to two weeks before the bid due date. If the parcel sells at auction, the county returns any net proceeds to the former owner. Occupants may still be living in parcels at the time of a fall auction, and the county lists occupant status with each parcel. The Treasurer's office asks that people not call for sale information, so read the Tax Deed Auction page first.

sections.h2: How do you sell a Dane County house with tax due?
sections.html:
Confirm the balance with the right treasurer, pay it at closing, and record the deed with the transfer return. Which treasurer you call depends on where the house is, because a Madison parcel and a parcel in Sun Prairie or Verona follow different collection routes.

  • Find the parcel number on the tax bill, or search Access Dane by address.
  • For Madison parcels, call the City of Madison Treasurer. For other parcels, ask the local municipal treasurer about tax due through January 31, and the Dane County Treasurer about the July 31 installment and any delinquent tax.
  • Record the deed at the Register of Deeds, phone (608) 266-4141, with the electronic Wisconsin Real Estate Transfer Return. The fee is 30 cents per $100 of value under Statute 77.22(1), charged to the grantor.
  • Update the mailing address after closing. Owner requests go in writing to Dane County Planning and Development, Property Listing, Room 116, or by email to property.listing@danecounty.gov.

When an owner has died, the county explains that the name comes off the record through a recorded Termination of Decedent's Interest for joint tenancy or survivorship marital property, or a Final Judgment for tenants in common. A transfer by will, descent or survivorship is exempt from the transfer fee under Statute 77.25(11).

faqs.q: When are Dane County property taxes due?
faqs.a: January 31 is the first due date and July 31 is the final due date. The January payment goes to your local municipality, and the July payment goes to the Dane County Treasurer, except for City of Madison properties, which the City Treasurer collects through July 31.

faqs.q: What penalty applies to late Dane County property tax?
faqs.a: Combined interest and penalty of 1.5% of the unpaid principal per month, added back to February 1. Once an installment is missed, the full amount is due immediately, and an August payment carries seven months of the charge, which is 10.5%.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Dane County property tax in person?
faqs.a: At the Dane County Treasurer's office in the City-County Building, Room 114, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison. Hours are 8:00 to 4:00 Monday through Friday, excluding holidays, and a drop box is available.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Dane County assessment after the Board of Review?
faqs.a: Usually not for that year. The county treasurer states that after the Board of Review it would normally be too late to appeal the assessed value. Talk to your assessor during the Open Book period and file with the board on time.

faqs.q: How do I change the billing address on a Dane County parcel?
faqs.a: Contact the municipal clerk or treasurer, or send a written request to Dane County Planning and Development, Property Listing, Room 116, 210 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Madison, WI 53703. Email to property.listing@danecounty.gov is also accepted.
